messages.subject: Re: nominal model constraint
messages.body_plain:
Hi KK,

You want to use the nominal.highlow parameter in your mirt() call.

For example,

# Set the nominal high/low matrix for 15 questions, with 2 as "high" and 1 as "low", and freely estimate the remaining categories.
nominal.highlow <- matrix(c(rep(2, 15), rep(1, 15)), 2, byrow = TRUE)

Then, when you call mirt, do something like:
mirt(data = dat, 1, itemtype = "nominal", nominal.highlow = nominal.highlow)

Of course, you don't have to use rep() and can set the high/low categories on an item by item basis.

messages.subject_clean: Comparison of factor scores of two-dimensional 2PL IRT model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I am struggling a bit as to how to interpret multipleGroup. I am assessing DIF with regard to stereotypes against two outgroups (Factor 1 and Factor 2) in three populations (US, UK, CA).

 I am trying to use (almost exactly) above model, i.e

model_constrained <- mirt.model('
F1 = 1-7
F2 = 8-14
COV = F1*F2
CONSTRAIN = (1-7, a1), (8-14, a2)')

group=c (rep ("D1", length (which (data$country=="US"))),
         rep ("D2", length (which (data$country=="UK"))),
         rep ("D3", length (which (data$country=="CA"))))

mod_metric <- multipleGroup(data[,119:132], model_constrained, group = group,SE=T)

My hope was to directly compare slope-parameters, For example, I would like to say that item one contributes "more" to Factor 1 in group "US" compared to group "UK" because its slope-parameter is more positive. However, running above model gives vastly different answers than running independent models (i.e. for group "US":

model_constrained <- mirt.model('
F1 = 1-7
F2 = 8-14
COV = F1*F2
CONSTRAIN = (1-7, a1), (8-14, a2)')
mod_metric <- mirt(data[which(data$country==US),119:132], model_constrained, group = group,SE=T)

and I am not sure what I miss. For example, running models separately reveals that perceptions of religious fanaticism are more important to Muslim-stereotyping in the US than in the UK (higher slope parameter), but the Multiple-group option yields the opposite result. I am sure it has something to do with the confirmatory nature of the model. When I run a simple exploratory model, i.e.

group=c (rep ("D1", length (which (data$country=="US"))),
         rep ("D2", length (which (data$country=="UK"))),
         rep ("D3", length (which (data$country=="CA"))))

mod_metric <- multipleGroup(data[,119:132], 1, group = group,SE=T)
mod_metric_separate <- mirt(data[which(data$country==US),119:132], 1, group = group,SE=T)
, the country-specific outputs of mod_metric are comparable with mod_metric_separate.

What am I missing?

Many thanks,
Tobi

It might be possible, but I don't (and won't support) it. MIRT models make much more sense in the slope intercept form to see the connection to non-linear factor analysis: a1 * theta1 + a2 * theta2 + dk, rather than some mix of weighted minus terms. I only included the classical IRT parameterization transformations for didactic purposes, but the whole package is built on the slope-intercept parameterizations for all models.

In many ways, I think the initial IRT models were misguided in their parameterization, because when you think that IRT is intimately connected to non-linear factor analysis then the a*(theta - b) approach seems rather counterintuitive and cumbersome (i.e., in a linear or logistic regression, you would never model your slopes and intercepts like that).

>

For polytomous items, I am used to provide the difficulty parameters in the ascendant order (the highest category being more difficult to answer than the lowest). Moreover, in my model I fixed constraints on the discrimination parameters and I considered what is called in the literature "between-items multidimensionality", so only one discrimination parameter is estimated for one item, the others being fixed to 0. Is this still a problem to get the IRT parameters ?

That's not a problem, but if there are several orthogonal factors you might benefit from using the bfactor() function to retain better numerical precision (or switch to the MHRM method). Cheers.

Phil

After spending some time in the literature following links in the blog.  I have come to the conclusion that both formulas are correct.  They however do represent different reliability coefficients. messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the pdf, Mark. I see what you are saying, but don't really understand the real purpose of the 'person separation' index. If one wants to compare individuals directly then you should do it directly, a la factor score estimates and their respective standard errors. No single composite is going to do better than the individual comparisons because it won't account for the respective variability of both response patterns (so a high person separation index might be very misleading in parts of the test where there is little information).

My usual argument also applies to these indices: they are generally useless when missing data are involved (which happens a lot, and is where IRT is actually quite useful due to its FIML nature). An individual who answers 10 versus 30 items will have a much higher SE, and there the reliability composite will be deflated for the test as a whole (shrunken estimate towards 0 + a larger SE). IMO, it makes more sense to look at information functions to determine the ultimate utility of the test because it might work better for some participants than others, and is obtainable regardless of the observed response patterns. Cheers.

Phil

Phil
